\chapter{Primero, Segundo, Tercero --- Counting in Order}
\label{ch:primero}
\hlchaptermodality{262}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say which one in a line something is.}

I can say which one in a line something is.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[primero · segundo · tercero]{primero · segundo · tercero — counting in order}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-primero}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Uno, dos, tres} — how many.

Now the other kind of counting: not how many, but \textbf{which one in the line}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Say them: \emph{\textbf{primero}}, \emph{\textbf{segundo}}, \emph{\textbf{tercero}}, \emph{\textbf{cuarto}}, \emph{\textbf{quinto}}.

And the second one has a story. Latin \emph{\textbf{secundus}} did not mean \emph{two}. It meant \textbf{following}, from the verb \emph{sequi}, \emph{to follow} — so second place is literally \emph{the one that comes after}. English \emph{second} is the very same word, and \emph{sequence} and \emph{consequence} are its cousins.

They behave as adjectives: \emph{la} \emph{\textbf{segunda}} \emph{casa}, \emph{los} \emph{\textbf{primeros}} \emph{libros}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{primero}, \emph{segundo}, \emph{tercero}, \emph{cuarto}, \emph{quinto}
  \item \emph{la segunda casa}, \emph{los primeros libros}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the first three in order. (\emph{\textbf{Primero}}, \emph{\textbf{segundo}}, \emph{\textbf{tercero}}.)

And what did \emph{secundus} mean before it meant \emph{second}? (\textbf{Following} — the one that comes after.) Next: where these words stand, and what happens to two of them when they get there.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el primer libro]{el primer libro — where an ordinal stands}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-primer-libro}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Primero}, \emph{segundo}, \emph{tercero}. And the rule you have carried for a long time: a Spanish adjective follows its noun.

These do not.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
Two things set them apart from ordinary adjectives.

\textbf{They go in front.} Where \emph{grande} follows its noun, an ordinal leads: \emph{el} \emph{\textbf{primer}} \emph{libro}, not \emph{el libro primero}.

And there — did you catch it? \emph{\textbf{Primer}}, not \emph{primero}. In front of a masculine singular noun, \emph{primero} and \emph{tercero} drop their final \emph{o}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{el} \emph{\textbf{primer}} \emph{libro} & but \emph{la} \emph{\textbf{primera}} \emph{casa} \\
\emph{el} \emph{\textbf{tercer}} \emph{libro} & but \emph{la} \emph{\textbf{tercera}} \emph{casa} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You have met this exact habit twice already: \emph{mucho} to \emph{muy}, and \emph{malo} to \emph{mal}. Three times now, so it is not a set of exceptions — it is what Spanish does to a word leaning on a masculine noun.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el primer libro}, \emph{la primera casa}
  \item \emph{muy}, \emph{mal}, \emph{primer} — one habit, three sightings
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does an ordinal stand? (\textbf{Before} the noun, unlike other adjectives.)

And which two lose their \emph{o}? (\emph{\textbf{Primero}} and \emph{\textbf{tercero}}, in front of a masculine noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
